items.title: Seabird ‘spies’ could help spot ships that aren’t broadcasting their location
items.summary:
A northern gannet ( Morus bassanus ) tagged with biologging devices on its back and tail Steve Votier 

Audio from seabirds fitted with mini recording devices and GPS trackers has been used by researchers to show that marine life can record encounters with vessels that are otherwise difficult to track.

Many large vessels are now legally required to carry automatic identification systems broadcasting their identity and location at regular intervals. Although this has allowed interactions between animals and fisheries to be studied at scale, there are enormous gaps in coverage.

In fact, recent research suggests that three-quarters of industrial fishing vessels don’t use the technology, says Jonathan Rutter at the University of Oxford. This is partly because regulations on the types of vessels that are required to share data vary by country. Large satellite ‘blind spots’ also contribute to the problem, he says, and so does subterfuge for the purpose of illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing (IUU).

Rutter says that being caught as bycatch in fishing is one of the greatest risks to seabird populations, but if fishing vessels are only tracked “with conventional methods, such footprints of risk may be strikingly incomplete”.

The team analysed audio collected from devices attached to seven northern gannets ( Morus bassanus ) and found that one third of the audio detections couldn’t be matched with vessel tracking data – mostly off the UK coast.

items.title: AI’s stunning progress in maths shows how little we understand it
items.summary:
MARK SYKES/SPL/Alamy 

There is a story, possibly apocryphal, that when the mathematician G. H. Hardy was about to undertake a dangerous sea voyage, he sent a postcard to a colleague declaring “I have solved the Riemann hypothesis”. Hardy, a staunch atheist, joked that this would prevent his ship from sinking, as God would never let him claim the credit for such a major result without revealing the details of his proof.

Hardy would probably be both astonished and aghast that we now have what seems to be a proof of the Riemann hypothesis , a problem that has vexed mathematicians since the 19th century, but that no one yet understands it. The consensus among mathematicians is that the proof, produced with the aid of AI, will hold, but that it will take much more work to make it comprehensible to humans.

However you feel about AI, this is a watershed moment, and one that demonstrates just how little we still understand about the capabilities of the technology. As recently as last month, leading mathematician Terence Tao speculated that AI would eventually solve the Riemann hypothesis, but that it may not happen before 2050. Now, some mathematicians are considering whether their hardest and most infamous remaining problems could be settled within months. In a year that has left mathematicians reeling, this may be the knock-out blow.

items.t: AI’s stunning progress in maths shows how little we understand it

items.title: Our verdict on Dark Eden by Chris Beckett: ‘Holy cow. Chapter 44!’
items.summary:
The New Scientist Book Club read Chris Beckett’s Dark Eden in November 

Since starting the New Scientist Book Club in May 2023, I have aimed to vary our books as much as possible, moving between science fiction and popular science, older classics and the hottest new titles. Occasionally, though, I’m afraid I let the power go to my head and just choose one of my own personal favourites. That’s what I did in November, with Chris Beckett’s novel Dark Eden , a book I’ve loved ever since it won the Arthur C. Clarke award in 2013.

Set on the planet Eden, a sunless world that drifts alone far outside the Milky Way, this follows the descendants of two astronauts who were marooned there over a century earlier. Now numbering 532 people, they tell each other stories of the world their ancestors came from, and struggle to survive on this dark, cold planet as they await the return of “one of those sky-boats with lights on them”. I think it is all wildly imaginative and original and exciting. So it was with some trepidation that I awaited the verdict of my fellow book club members on our Discord channel. I really wanted everyone else to love it, too!

items.title: Is The Time Traveler’s Wife the perfect audiobook to experience on shuffle?
items.summary:
Josie Ford 

Feedback is our weekly column of bizarre stories, implausible advertising claims, confusing instructions and more 

Reader Jenny Ozanne writes to tell us of a horrific incident that befell her partner. He had bought Audrey Niffenegger’s novel The Time Traveler’s Wife as a CD audiobook, to listen to on long car journeys.

“After a while, he complained that the plot was completely impossible to follow,” writes Jenny. “It was only when I checked his player that I realized he had accidentally set the CD to ‘shuffle’. “

Advertisement 

Jenny raises two points, which Feedback heartily endorses: “I’m still not sure what’s more impressive: the story’s ability to survive total chronological chaos, or the fact that he listened to three random chapters before suspecting anything was wrong.”

Feedback would suggest that The Time Traveler’s Wife might be the ideal novel to experience on shuffle, since the narrative is heavily non-linear. The main character hops uncontrollably back and forth through history. This led us to wonder: would any similarly chrono-displaced stories survive the experience of being played on shuffle, or even be improved by it?

We wondered, for instance, about David Mitchell’s Cloud Atlas . This has six stories set in different periods, including a future in which human clones are used as cheap labour, and a more distant future in which everything has gone a bit Mad Max . The stories are linked by characters in later timelines reading about the earlier ones, and by subtle coincidences. What would it be like on shuffle?

However, after careful…

items.title: Australia’s legless geckos evolved like snakes did
items.summary: Pygopods — Australia’s limbless geckos — have taken an evolutionary path more like that of snakes than of other legless lizards.

items.title: A space telescope hunting for dark matter just discovered something unexpected
items.summary: ESA’s Euclid space telescope has discovered its first previously unknown comet, despite being designed to study distant galaxies and the mysteries of the dark Universe. The icy object is approximately 1.3 billion kilometers from Earth and follows an unusual orbit that takes thousands of years to complete.
items.t: A space telescope hunting for dark matter just discovered something unexpected

items.title: Physicists trap antimatter in a breakthrough that could explain why the universe exists
items.summary: Positrons are the antimatter counterpart of an electron. Physicists trapped a positron and cooled it to temperatures near absolute zero. Positron is suspended in a wall-free trap, safely separated from ordinary matter. Team will conduct most precise comparison yet between matter and antimatter. Any difference between the electron and positron could expose cracks in the Standard Model of particle physics.
items.t: Physicists trap antimatter in a breakthrough that could explain why the universe exists

items.title: What is a thought made of? Why human consciousness may be beyond AI’s reach
items.summary: A new theory suggests that the brain may chemically encode and retrieve memories rather than relying solely on electrical signals. Researchers propose that interactions between brain cells and their molecular surroundings could help explain the intimate connection between memory, emotion, and thought. Their findings challenge the assumption that increasingly powerful computers could eventually develop human-like consciousness.
items.t: What is a thought made of? Why human consciousness may be beyond AI’s reach

items.title: Physicists just sent an unblockable message through a brick wall using gravity
items.summary: Scientists have successfully transmitted a message through a brick wall using nothing but gravity, an old elevator, and an incredibly sensitive detector. By moving a massive counterweight between two positions, researchers encoded the word "Gravity" into tiny changes in gravitational pull. Unlike Wi-Fi or radio signals, gravity passes through ordinary barriers without being blocked, offering a potentially revolutionary way to communicate.
items.t: Physicists just sent an unblockable message through a brick wall using gravity

items.title: Einstein’s 120-year-old theory may be missing something big about the Big Bang
items.summary: A surprising discovery by MIT and UC Santa Barbara physicists reveals that Einstein’s famous theory of particle motion misses something important when particles travel near the speed of light. Their new calculations show that heavy quarks moving through an ultra-hot plasma experience rare but unusually powerful jolts that Einstein’s traditional model cannot fully explain.
items.t: Einstein’s 120-year-old theory may be missing something big about the Big Bang

items.title: Extinct, long-legged grasshoppers walked on water alongside dinosaurs
items.summary: Clues in 99-million-year-old amber show why scientists think these insects could sit atop water and paddle across it.
items.t: Extinct, long-legged grasshoppers walked on water alongside dinosaurs

items.title: New nose drops restore youthful memory and fight Alzheimer’s in aging mice
items.summary: A revolutionary new nasal treatment has restored youthful learning and memory performance in aging mice while preventing severe cognitive decline in mice with Alzheimer’s-like disease. Developed using technology similar to COVID-19 mRNA vaccines, the nose drops stimulate production of a brain-protecting protein that strengthens neurons and supports memory. Remarkably, the treatment preserved brain function without removing Alzheimer’s-associated plaques, suggesting a completely different way to combat cognitive decline.
items.t: New nose drops restore youthful memory and fight Alzheimer’s in aging mice

items.title: A black hole the size of an atom could destroy an entire star
items.summary: MIT scientists have discovered that tiny black holes left over from the Big Bang could slowly devour stars from within, eventually triggering spectacular explosions visible across galaxies. Detecting these unusual cosmic events could reveal the existence of primordial black holes and help solve the mystery of dark matter.
items.t: A black hole the size of an atom could destroy an entire star

items.title: This man sometimes sees his cat’s eyes on people’s faces
items.summary: After brain surgery, he began seeing eyes he’d recently seen on other’s faces. The rare condition is providing insight into how brains perceive faces.
items.t: This man sometimes sees his cat’s eyes on people’s faces

items.title: Eagles can prey on adult baboons. Did our ancestors face that threat?
items.summary: Baboon remains with talon injuries reveal eagles can hunt large primates, suggesting human ancestors developed tactics to guard against such attacks.
items.t: Eagles can prey on adult baboons. Did our ancestors face that threat?

items.title: 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck reveals an ingenious waterproofing trick
items.summary: A 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck has revealed sophisticated waterproofing techniques involving pine tar and beeswax. Microscopic pollen grains trapped in the ancient coatings are now helping scientists reconstruct where the vessel may have traveled and undergone repairs more than two millennia ago.
items.t: 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck reveals an ingenious waterproofing trick

items.title: Ancient rocks from the Moon’s far side rewrite the Solar System’s violent past
items.summary: Scientists studying ancient rocks from the Moon’s far side have uncovered surprising evidence that challenges decades of thinking about the Solar System’s violent past. Instead of a single catastrophic bombardment, asteroid impacts appear to have declined gradually over billions of years, revealing new clues about Earth's early evolution and the origins of life.
items.t: Ancient rocks from the Moon’s far side rewrite the Solar System’s violent past

items.title: Earth's next ice age may have already begun. Global warming stopped it
items.summary: Scientists have uncovered surprising evidence that Earth’s next ice age may have already begun, only to be stopped by global warming. By studying ancient plants preserved beneath the Barnes Ice Cap in the Canadian Arctic, researchers discovered that the remnants of a massive ice sheet began expanding again about 2,000 years ago, signaling the possible start of a new glacial period. But by the 1960s, rising temperatures had reversed that growth, causing the ice to shrink instead.
items.t: Earth's next ice age may have already begun. Global warming stopped it

items.title: Earth’s ancient oceans may have fooled scientists about its oxygen history
items.summary: Earth’s journey from an oxygen-starved world to a planet capable of supporting complex life may have unfolded very differently than scientists once believed. A new analysis suggests that oxygen accumulated in the atmosphere in three major stages, with the oceans taking millions or even hundreds of millions of years to catch up.
items.t: Earth’s ancient oceans may have fooled scientists about its oxygen history

items.title: Math’s holy grail, the Riemann hypothesis, appears solved with AI’s help
items.summary: The proof apparently settles a 167-year-old puzzle related to prime numbers, thanks to a human mathematician working with AI.
items.t: Math’s holy grail, the Riemann hypothesis, appears solved with AI’s help

items.title: The notion of ‘positive masculinity’ is dividing the male studies field
items.summary: Masculinity has long been seen as a problem to be solved. Researchers disagree on how to flip the script so as to help men improve well-being.
items.t: The notion of ‘positive masculinity’ is dividing the male studies field

Of course, mutation is allowed, as is the genetic mixing and matching of sexual reproduction, to create variety and evolutionary diversity. But we all exist because a viable lineage of DNA has persisted for 4 billion years. The genome’s policy is typically…

items.title: ‘Mitt & Ted’ recounts how a political odd couple changed U.S. health care
items.summary: The newest season of The Big Dig podcast tells of how Mitt Romney and Ted Kennedy briefly joined forces to reform healthcare laws.
items.t: ‘Mitt & Ted’ recounts how a political odd couple changed U.S. healthcare

items.title: A galactic shock wave could rewrite the map of the Milky Way
items.summary: A surprising discovery suggests the Milky Way may be making stars in places where most galaxies cannot. Scientists found evidence that a massive rotating structure near the galactic center is creating powerful shock waves that trigger star formation rather than suppress it. Even more unexpectedly, part of the Norma spiral arm may not be a spiral arm at all, but a vast region where new stars are being born.
items.t: A galactic shock wave could rewrite the map of the Milky Way

items.title: Two monster black holes from the dawn of time defy explanation
items.summary: Astronomers have discovered the oldest known compact pair of quasars, powered by two enormous black holes that existed just 900 million years after the Big Bang. Weighing an astonishing 1.5 billion and 400 million times the mass of the Sun, these cosmic giants somehow grew to incredible sizes far earlier than current theories can explain.
items.t: Two monster black holes from the dawn of time defy explanation

items.title: Mysterious new viruses reveal a missing link in evolution
items.summary: Scientists have discovered previously unknown viruses that could help explain how some of life’s earliest biological structures evolved. The surprising findings challenge a longstanding evolutionary theory and suggest that viruses may have hidden capabilities far beyond simply infecting cells.
items.t: Mysterious new viruses reveal a missing link in evolution

items.title: Earth's core may be leaking a 4.5-billion-year-old secret
items.summary: Scientists have discovered an unusual carbon signature in Hawaiian volcanic rocks that suggests some of Earth's carbon originated in ancient meteorites and later escaped from deep within the planet's core. The discovery raises an astonishing possibility: Carbon essential to life may have traveled from space to Earth's depths before emerging through volcanoes billions of years later.
items.t: Earth's core may be leaking a 4.5-billion-year-old secret

items.title: Archaeologists reveal a powerful Iron Age king may have been a woman
items.summary: Archaeologists have uncovered evidence that Verica, the Iron Age ruler whose exile helped trigger Rome’s invasion of Britain in AD 43, was actually a woman. The discovery challenges centuries of historical assumptions and suggests that a largely forgotten female leader may have changed the course of British history.
items.t: Archaeologists reveal a powerful Iron Age king may have been a woman

items.title: Motion under the ocean explains the depth of the world’s deepest spot
items.summary: The deepest known remnants of explosive volcanism offer a new clue to how Challenger Deep became the ocean's deepest point.
items.t: Motion under the ocean explains the depth of the world’s deepest spot

items.title: This tiny spider named after Stephen Colbert has a genome 50% larger than a human’s
items.summary: A tiny California trapdoor spider named after Stephen Colbert has a genome roughly 50% larger than a human's, despite being only about the size of a quarter. Scientists discovered that its enormous genome contains 4.6 billion DNA base pairs and 52 chromosomes, revealing surprising clues about spider evolution.
items.t: This tiny spider named after Stephen Colbert has a genome 50% larger than a human’s

items.title: A mysterious gap hints at black holes born from stars that never exploded
items.summary: Massive stars may be quietly collapsing into black holes without ever producing the spectacular supernova explosions scientists typically expect. A surprising pattern in 257 black hole mergers suggests these mysterious stellar disappearances could explain the origins of a large population of black holes throughout the universe.
items.t: A mysterious gap hints at black holes born from stars that never exploded

items.title: DNA’s secret sunscreen may have helped life survive on early Earth
items.summary: Scientists have uncovered a surprising reason why early life may have survived Earth's intense ultraviolet radiation: a key component of DNA appears to turn potentially destructive damage into something easier to repair. The discovery could help solve a decades-old evolutionary mystery and reveal how life endured the harsh conditions of our planet's earliest days.
items.t: DNA’s secret sunscreen may have helped life survive on early Earth

items.title: A 194-year-old tortoise has a remarkable anti-aging secret hidden in its DNA
items.summary: At an astonishing 194 years old, Jonathan the giant tortoise is the world's oldest living land animal, and scientists may have finally uncovered the secrets behind his extraordinary lifespan. Researchers identified 287 unique genetic variants linked to processes that help repair damaged DNA, control inflammation, regulate insulin, and suppress cancer.
items.t: A 194-year-old tortoise has a remarkable anti-aging secret hidden in its DNA

items.title: Time may be far stranger than we realize. Scientists have a way to test it
items.summary: Time may be far stranger than we realize, and scientists have proposed a way to detect clocks experiencing multiple flows of time simultaneously. Using atomic clocks with dramatically enhanced sensitivity, researchers hope to reveal a never-before-observed quantum effect that could transform our understanding of time and gravity.
items.t: Time may be far stranger than we realize. Scientists have a way to test it

items.title: A giant star swallowed another star. James Webb reveals the aftermath
items.summary: Astronomers have witnessed a spectacular cosmic collision in the Andromeda galaxy, where a small star spiraled into a giant star 18,000 times brighter than the Sun, triggering a violent eruption. NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope captured the aftermath just 47 days later, revealing new details about how two stars can merge into one.
items.t: A giant star swallowed another star. James Webb reveals the aftermath

items.title: Astronomer Isabel Angelo hunts for odd signals in telescope data
items.summary: At the SETI Institute, she uses machine learning to look for signs of cosmic phenomena astronomers have never seen before.
items.t: Astronomer Isabel Angelo hunts for odd signals in telescope data

items.title: This scientist proves which problems computers can’t solve quickly
items.summary: Dor Minzer studies how fast computers can tell whether nearly all of a game’s rules can be satisfied or almost none can.
items.t: This scientist proves which problems computers can’t solve quickly

items.title: What helps land recover after fire? This ecologist looks to the past
items.summary: Ecologist Jennifer Grenz draws on Indigenous oral histories and ecological records to learn how landscapes recover after wildfires.
items.t: What helps land recover after fire? This ecologist looks to the past

items.title: How do scientists learn from failure? This researcher has clues
items.summary: Yian Yin found that scientists who revised rejected proposals using feedback found success faster than those who switched ideas.
items.t: How do scientists learn from failure? This researcher has clues

items.title: How do tumors talk to nerves? This scientist is finding out
items.summary: After finding proteins linked to memory in prostate cancer cells, Sebnem Ece Eksi hopes to map nerve fibers in tumors.
items.t: How do tumors talk to nerves? This scientist is finding out

items.title: After 8 years in space, a groundbreaking X-ray telescope finally opens its eyes
items.summary: After eight years and 10 billion kilometers in space, a groundbreaking X-ray telescope heading to Mercury has captured its first cosmic observations and is performing even better than scientists expected. The instrument could soon reveal Mercury's hidden chemical secrets and transform our understanding of how the solar system's smallest planet formed.
items.t: After 8 years in space, a groundbreaking X-ray telescope finally opens its eyes
